points_json.example: Feeling nervous before a job interview is normal anxiety. Refusing to ever apply for jobs because interviews terrify you is an anxiety disorder.
points_json.point: Fear and anxiety are different. Fear is a response to a real, immediate threat (a dog running at you). Anxiety is worry about a future threat that may never come (worrying all week about Friday's exam). Anxiety disorders happen when fear or anxiety becomes excessive and disrupts daily life.

points_json.example: A 9-year-old who cries every morning, clings to her mother, and refuses to go to school because she fears her mother will get hurt while she is away.
points_json.point: Separation Anxiety Disorder is excessive fear about being separated from attachment figures (parents, partners). The person worries something bad will happen to them, refuses to leave home or sleep alone, and may have nightmares about separation. It must last at least 4 weeks in children and 6 months in adults.

points_json.example: A 6-year-old who chats happily with family at home but has not said a single word in her classroom for the whole school year.
points_json.point: Selective Mutism is when a child consistently fails to speak in specific social situations (like school) even though they speak normally at home. It is not shyness or defiance — the child is frozen by anxiety. It usually appears before age 5.

points_json.example: A student who takes a 2-hour bus route to avoid a 10-minute bridge crossing because of a fear of heights.
points_json.point: Specific Phobia is an intense, irrational fear of a specific object or situation — animals, heights, blood, flying, enclosed spaces. The person knows the fear is unreasonable but avoids the trigger anyway, and even thinking about it causes panic.

points_json.example: A university student who drops a course because it requires a class presentation, even though she needs it to graduate.
points_json.point: Social Anxiety Disorder (social phobia) is a strong fear of social situations where the person might be judged, embarrassed, or watched — speaking in public, eating in front of others, meeting new people. They fear they will act in a way that brings shame.

points_json.example: A man who had a panic attack in a shopping mall now avoids all malls, cinemas, and crowded markets, fearing another attack.
points_json.point: Panic Disorder means repeated, unexpected panic attacks — sudden surges of intense fear with a racing heart, sweating, shaking, shortness of breath, and a feeling of dying or losing control. After an attack, the person lives in worry about the next one and avoids places where escape feels hard.

points_json.example: A woman who has not left her house alone in two years and only goes out when her brother walks with her.
points_json.point: Agoraphobia is fear of situations where escape might be difficult or help unavailable during panic — public transport, open spaces, closed spaces, crowds, or being outside home alone. About half of people with panic disorder also develop agoraphobia.

points_json.example: A mother who lies awake every night worrying about her children's safety, their grades, and the family's finances, even though nothing is actually wrong.
points_json.point: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is excessive, uncontrollable worry about many everyday things — health, money, family, work — happening more days than not for at least 6 months. It comes with restlessness, tiredness, trouble concentrating, irritability, muscle tension, and poor sleep.

points_json.example: A child bitten by a dog once may develop a lifelong dog phobia because the brain linked dogs with pain.
points_json.point: Causes of anxiety disorders: genetics (they run in families), brain chemistry (an overactive amygdala, the brain's alarm system, and low GABA or serotonin), temperament (shy, easily upset children are at higher risk), and learning (a bad experience teaches the brain to fear — classical conditioning).

points_json.example: A person afraid of elevators first looks at pictures of elevators, then stands near one, then rides one floor — step by step until the fear is gone.
points_json.point: Treatments that work: CBT (cognitive-behavioral therapy) teaches people to challenge scary thoughts; exposure therapy gradually faces the feared situation until the fear fades; and medicines like SSRIs calm the brain's alarm system. Exposure is the gold standard for phobias.

summary: Fear and worry gone too far. This note covers every DSM-5-TR anxiety disorder — from specific phobias and social anxiety to panic disorder and GAD — plus causes and treatments, in simple words.
title: Anxiety Disorders (DSM-5-TR)

points_json.example: Someone who has distrusted every friend, partner, and coworker for 15 years — not because people betrayed them, but because distrust is their fixed way of seeing the world.
points_json.point: A personality disorder is an enduring, inflexible pattern of thinking, feeling, and behaving that differs sharply from what the person's culture expects. It causes serious problems in relationships and work, starts by early adulthood, and is stable over time — it is not a passing phase.

points_json.example: Think of it as: Cluster A = strange, Cluster B = wild, Cluster C = worried.
points_json.point: DSM-5-TR groups the 10 personality disorders into 3 clusters. Cluster A is odd and eccentric behavior. Cluster B is dramatic, emotional, and unpredictable behavior. Cluster C is anxious and fearful behavior.

points_json.example: An employee who believes his coworkers' casual jokes are secret plans to get him fired.
points_json.point: Cluster A: Paranoid Personality Disorder means deep distrust — the person believes others are lying, cheating, or plotting against them, reads hidden threats into innocent remarks, and never forgives insults.

points_json.example: A schizoid man lives alone, works night shifts to avoid people, and feels fine about it. A schizotypal woman believes she can read minds and talks in strange, vague riddles.
points_json.point: Cluster A continued: Schizoid Personality Disorder means the person genuinely prefers to be alone, has little interest in relationships or sex, and shows almost no emotion. Schizotypal Personality Disorder adds strange beliefs, magical thinking, and odd speech or behavior.

points_json.example: A man who scams elderly people out of savings, gets arrested, and blames the victims for being foolish.
points_json.point: Cluster B: Antisocial Personality Disorder means a long pattern of ignoring the rights of others — lying, cheating, aggression, and no guilt or remorse. It can only be diagnosed at 18+, and there must be conduct problems before age 15.

points_json.example: A woman who idealizes her new friend as perfect on Monday, then hates her as cruel on Wednesday because she replied late to a message.
points_json.point: Cluster B continued: Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) means unstable relationships, unstable self-image, and unstable emotions, plus impulsivity. Signs include frantic efforts to avoid abandonment, self-harm, intense anger, and chronic emptiness.

points_json.example: A histrionic student who cries loudly in class over small issues so everyone looks at her. A narcissistic boss who takes credit for all team work and calls struggling employees weak.
points_json.point: Cluster B continued: Histrionic Personality Disorder means attention-seeking — dramatic emotions, flirting, and feeling uncomfortable when not the center of attention. Narcissistic Personality Disorder means grandiosity, a constant need for admiration, and a lack of empathy.

points_json.example: An avoidant graduate who never applies for jobs fearing rejection. A dependent woman who asks her sister what to wear, eat, and whom to marry.
points_json.point: Cluster C: Avoidant Personality Disorder means the person desperately wants relationships but avoids them from fear of criticism and rejection — extreme shyness that ruins life. Dependent Personality Disorder means the person cannot make even small decisions alone and clings to others.

points_json.example: A manager who rewrites every team report himself because nobody meets his impossible standards, then misses every deadline.
points_json.point: Cluster C continued: Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder (OCPD) means extreme perfectionism, orderliness, and control — not the same as OCD. There are no true obsessions or compulsions, just a rigid need for everything to be done their way.

points_json.example: A BPD patient in DBT learns skills to survive intense emotions without self-harm — like holding ice cubes instead of cutting when the pain feels unbearable.
points_json.point: Causes include genetics, childhood trauma or neglect, and parenting styles. Treatment is mainly long-term psychotherapy — DBT (dialectical behavior therapy) was designed for borderline PD and strongly reduces self-harm. Medicines treat symptoms like depression, not the disorder itself.

summary: Deeply rooted patterns of thinking and behaving that clash with everyday life. This note explains all 10 DSM-5-TR personality disorders across Clusters A, B, and C, with causes and treatments.
title: Personality Disorders (DSM-5-TR)

points_json.example: A student who loved cricket now feels empty, cannot get out of bed, has stopped eating, and cries daily for three weeks — this goes beyond normal sadness.
points_json.point: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) needs 5 or more symptoms for at least 2 weeks, and one of them must be depressed mood or loss of interest/pleasure (anhedonia). The symptoms must hurt daily life and not be caused by drugs or another medical condition.

points_json.example: Remember it as: mood, interest, appetite, sleep, movement, energy, guilt, concentration, death.
points_json.point: The 9 key symptoms of MDD: depressed mood most of the day, loss of interest in almost everything, big weight/appetite change, sleep problems (too much or too little), restlessness or slowness, fatigue, worthlessness or guilt, trouble concentrating, and thoughts of death or suicide.

points_json.example: A man who has felt low, tired, and hopeless almost every day for 3 years, yet still goes to work — he thinks this is just his personality.
points_json.point: Persistent Depressive Disorder (dysthymia) is a milder but longer depression — depressed mood more days than not for at least 2 years (1 year in children). The person may function, but life always feels grey and joyless.

points_json.example: A 9-year-old who explodes into hour-long screaming tantrums 4 times a week over tiny issues like the wrong breakfast.
points_json.point: Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder (DMDD) is diagnosed in children 6–18 with severe, repeated temper outbursts and a constantly irritable mood between outbursts. It was added to stop over-diagnosing bipolar disorder in angry children.

points_json.example: A woman who becomes severely depressed and hopeless for 5 days every month, then feels completely normal once her period begins.
points_json.point: Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD) is a severe form of PMS — in the week before periods, the woman has intense mood swings, anger, anxiety, or depression that vanish after bleeding starts. It is a real disorder, not just bad PMS.

points_json.example: A new mother who cries all day, feels she is a bad mother, and cannot bond with her baby may have peripartum depression.
points_json.point: Depression has specifiers: melancholic (worst in mornings, no pleasure at all), atypical (mood lifts with good news, sleeps/eats more), psychotic (with delusions), seasonal pattern (winter depression), and peripartum onset (during pregnancy or after birth).

points_json.example: If a parent has severe depression, the child's risk is 2–3 times higher than average.
points_json.point: Biological causes: low serotonin and norepinephrine, an overactive stress system (cortisol), smaller hippocampus, genetics (depression runs in families), and medical issues like thyroid problems or vitamin D deficiency.

points_json.example: Failing one test becomes 'I am a total failure and will never succeed at anything.'
points_json.point: Beck's cognitive theory says depression comes from the negative triad — hopeless thoughts about the self ('I am worthless'), the world ('life is unfair'), and the future ('nothing will improve') — plus thinking errors like seeing everything in black and white.

points_json.example: A student who failed twice stops studying completely, saying 'what is the point, I will fail anyway.'
points_json.point: Learned helplessness (Seligman) says that after repeated uncontrollable bad events, people stop trying — they learn that nothing they do matters. This passive giving-up looks exactly like depression.

points_json.example: A depressed patient starts with a 10-minute daily walk and one phone call to a friend — small steps that slowly restart the brain's reward system.
points_json.point: Treatments: CBT challenges negative thoughts, behavioral activation rebuilds daily routines and pleasant activities, antidepressants (SSRIs) rebalance brain chemistry, exercise works as well as medicine for mild cases, and ECT helps severe, treatment-resistant depression.

summary: More than sadness — depression changes mood, body, and thinking. This note covers Major Depressive Disorder, Persistent Depressive Disorder, DMDD, PMDD, causes, and treatments in simple words.
title: Depressive Disorders (DSM-5-TR)

points_json.example: A woman who washes her hands 40 times a day until they bleed because she cannot shake the thought that germs will kill her family.
points_json.point: OCD has two parts. Obsessions are unwanted, intrusive thoughts or images that cause anxiety (fear of germs, fear of harming someone). Compulsions are repetitive behaviors the person feels forced to do to reduce that anxiety (washing, checking, counting). The person usually knows these are excessive but cannot stop.

points_json.example: A man who checks his front door lock 20 times every night and is always late for work because of it.
points_json.point: Common OCD themes: contamination (cleaning), doubt and checking (locks, stove), symmetry and ordering, forbidden thoughts (aggressive or religious), and hoarding urges. Compulsions eat hours daily and the person feels trapped by them.

points_json.example: A girl with a normal nose who has had 3 nose surgeries and still cries daily believing her nose is deformed.
points_json.point: Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD) means the person is obsessed with a small or imagined flaw in their appearance — nose, skin, hair — and spends hours mirror-checking, comparing, or seeking cosmetic surgery that never satisfies them.

points_json.example: An elderly man whose house is filled floor-to-ceiling with old magazines, leaving only narrow paths to walk through.
points_json.point: Hoarding Disorder is the persistent difficulty throwing away possessions — old newspapers, broken items, trash — because of a strong need to save them and distress at discarding them. Homes become unlivable and unsafe.

points_json.example: A student who pulls out her eyebrows during exam stress until they are completely gone.
points_json.point: Trichotillomania (hair-pulling disorder) and Excoriation (skin-picking disorder) involve repeatedly pulling out hair or picking skin, causing bald spots or wounds. The person tries to stop but the urge feels irresistible, especially during stress or boredom.

points_json.example: Checking the lock reduces anxiety for 5 minutes, so the brain learns: checking = relief. The cycle strengthens.
points_json.point: Causes: genetics, low serotonin, an overactive brain circuit between the orbitofrontal cortex and basal ganglia (the brain's worry loop gets stuck), and learning — compulsions are negatively reinforced because they briefly reduce anxiety.

points_json.example: A contamination-OCD patient touches a public railing and waits without washing. After 30 minutes the anxiety fades on its own — proof the danger was imagined.
points_json.point: The best treatment is ERP — Exposure and Response Prevention. The person faces the feared situation (touches a doorknob) and is prevented from doing the compulsion (no washing). Anxiety spikes, then naturally falls — teaching the brain the fear was false.

points_json.example: A BDD patient practices describing her whole face neutrally in the mirror instead of zooming in on the hated nose for an hour.
points_json.point: Medicines (SSRIs at higher doses than for depression) also help OCD, and CBT adds thought-challenging skills. For BDD, mirror-retraining and stopping reassurance-seeking are key. Hoarding treatment focuses on sorting practice and decision-making skills.

summary: Unwanted thoughts and irresistible rituals. This note explains OCD, body dysmorphic disorder, hoarding, hair-pulling, and skin-picking — plus the famous ERP treatment — in simple words.
title: OCD and Related Disorders (DSM-5-TR)

points_json.example: A 22-year-old university student who was doing well suddenly insists the TV is sending him secret messages and stops attending classes.
points_json.point: Schizophrenia is a severe disorder where the person loses touch with reality. Diagnosis needs 2 or more key symptoms for at least 6 months, with clear decline in work, relationships, or self-care. It affects about 1 in 100 people and usually appears in late teens to early 30s.

points_json.example: A patient hears two voices commenting on everything she does, and believes her neighbors planted cameras in her walls.
points_json.point: Positive symptoms (extra experiences added): delusions — fixed false beliefs (being spied on, having special powers); hallucinations — hearing voices is most common; disorganized speech — jumping between unrelated topics; and disorganized or catatonic behavior.

points_json.example: A man who sits silently all day, shows no expression when his sister visits, and has stopped showering or eating properly.
points_json.point: Negative symptoms (things taken away): flat emotions, very little speech, no motivation, inability to feel pleasure, and social withdrawal. These are harder to treat and hurt daily life the most.

points_json.example: A patient who cannot follow a 3-step cooking recipe she once knew by heart.
points_json.point: Cognitive symptoms: poor attention, weak memory, and trouble planning or making decisions. The person may struggle to follow a conversation or hold a simple job.

points_json.example: A woman who functions perfectly at work but is convinced her boss is secretly in love with her despite zero evidence (erotomanic type).
points_json.point: Delusional Disorder means holding one strong delusion (being followed, being loved by a celebrity, having a disease) for at least a month, but otherwise thinking and behavior look normal — unlike schizophrenia.

points_json.example: A man who develops delusions and hallucinations for 3 weeks after his brother's sudden death, then fully recovers.
points_json.point: Brief Psychotic Disorder lasts less than a month (often after extreme stress) and full recovery is expected. Schizophreniform Disorder looks like schizophrenia but lasts 1–6 months. Schizoaffective Disorder mixes schizophrenia symptoms with a major mood episode (depression or mania).

points_json.example: Drugs like cocaine that raise dopamine can trigger temporary psychosis-like symptoms, supporting the dopamine link.
points_json.point: The dopamine hypothesis says schizophrenia involves too much dopamine activity in some brain areas — this is why antipsychotic drugs that block dopamine reduce hallucinations and delusions. Brain scans also show larger ventricles and smaller frontal lobes.

points_json.example: Adoption studies show children of schizophrenic parents raised by healthy families still carry higher risk — pointing to genes, not just upbringing.
points_json.point: Genetics matter strongly: if an identical twin has schizophrenia, the other twin's risk is about 50%. Prenatal risks include mother's infections, malnutrition, and birth complications. Stressful life events can trigger episodes in vulnerable people.

points_json.example: A patient stable for a year stops his tablets feeling cured — within weeks the voices return.
points_json.point: Treatment: antipsychotic medicines are the foundation — they control positive symptoms but have side effects like weight gain and stiffness. Newer (atypical) antipsychotics are preferred. Stopping medicine is the top cause of relapse.

points_json.example: A recovered patient works part-time with a job coach while attending a weekly social skills group — living independently, not just surviving.
points_json.point: Psychosocial treatments complete the picture: family therapy reduces relapse, social skills training rebuilds daily functioning, supported employment helps patients work, and CBT for psychosis challenges distressing delusions.

summary: When reality itself breaks down. This note explains schizophrenia's positive, negative, and cognitive symptoms, related psychotic disorders, causes, and treatments in simple words.
title: Schizophrenia Spectrum (DSM-5-TR)

points_json.example: A soldier who survives a bomb blast, a woman assaulted at night, or a firefighter who recovers bodies from a disaster site.
points_json.point: PTSD (Posttraumatic Stress Disorder) develops after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence — directly experiencing it, witnessing it, learning it happened to a loved one, or repeated exposure (like rescue workers). Not every trauma causes PTSD; most people recover naturally.

points_json.example: A car-crash survivor who breaks into a cold sweat and relives the crash every time she hears brakes screech.
points_json.point: Symptom group 1 — Intrusion: the trauma keeps invading the mind through nightmares, flashbacks (feeling it is happening again), and intense distress at reminders. The person cannot simply forget it.

points_json.example: An assault survivor who stops going out after dark, avoids the street where it happened, and refuses to talk about that night.
points_json.point: Symptom group 2 — Avoidance: the person avoids everything linked to the trauma — places, people, conversations, even thoughts and feelings about it. Their world shrinks as avoidance grows.

points_json.example: A survivor who believes the attack was her fault for walking alone, and has stopped meeting her best friends.
points_json.point: Symptom group 3 — Negative changes in mood and thinking: blaming oneself, feeling detached from loved ones, inability to feel happiness, and a dark view of the world ('no one can be trusted').

points_json.example: A veteran who dives under the table when a balloon pops at a birthday party.
points_json.point: Symptom group 4 — Hyperarousal: the body stays on high alert — irritability, angry outbursts, reckless behavior, being easily startled, trouble concentrating, and broken sleep.

points_json.example: Two weeks after an earthquake, a man still has nightmares and cannot enter buildings — this is acute stress disorder; if it continues past a month, it becomes PTSD.
points_json.point: PTSD needs symptoms from all four groups lasting more than 1 month and disrupting daily life. Acute Stress Disorder is the same picture but lasts 3 days to 1 month right after the trauma — many (not all) cases turn into PTSD.

points_json.example: A student who fails an exam and becomes tearful, sleepless, and unable to study for two months.
points_json.point: Adjustment Disorders are milder stress responses — emotional or behavior symptoms after an identifiable stressor (divorce, job loss, moving) that are stronger than expected but do not meet criteria for other disorders. They resolve within 6 months after the stressor ends.

points_json.example: Two soldiers survive the same battle — the one with supportive family and friends recovers, the isolated one develops PTSD.
points_json.point: Risk factors for PTSD: severity of the trauma, prior trauma or childhood abuse, lack of social support afterward, family history of mental illness, and dissociation during the event (feeling unreal or detached as it happened).

points_json.example: In prolonged exposure, a survivor describes the assault in detail session after session — by week 8, telling the story no longer causes panic.
points_json.point: The best treatments: trauma-focused CBT helps patients process the memory safely, prolonged exposure revisits the trauma memory until it loses power, and EMDR uses guided eye movements while recalling the trauma. SSRIs also reduce symptoms.

points_json.example: The most healing sentence a friend can say: 'I believe you, and I am here for as long as you need.'
points_json.point: What does NOT help: forcing someone to talk before they are ready, or saying 'just forget it and move on.' What helps: safety, patience, professional help, and supportive people who listen without judgment.

summary: When a terrible event keeps haunting the mind. This note covers PTSD's four symptom groups, acute stress disorder, adjustment disorders, risk factors, and proven treatments in simple words.
title: Trauma and Stressor-Related Disorders (DSM-5-TR)
